rules.title: Government or regulatory impersonation
rules.why: Tax, KYC, customs and utility scams impersonate authorities because people comply with official-sounding demands, especially under a deadline.
rules.advice: Government bodies do not collect fees or IDs by email link. Check on the official government portal by typing its address yourself.
examples: Your Aadhaar will be deactivated unless you link your PAN - pay the update fee here.
falsePositives: Genuine government notifications exist; they point to a portal you can reach by typing its official address.

rules.title: IT helpdesk impersonation
rules.why: Impersonating IT support ('mailbox full', 'password expires today') is a common way to get staff to hand over credentials over email or phone.
rules.advice: IT never asks for your password. Verify with your IT team through a channel you already use.
examples: Your mailbox storage is full. Click here to upgrade and avoid losing emails.
falsePositives: Real IT notices exist but never ask for credentials; combine with sender and link analysis.

rules.title: Executive or authority impersonation (BEC)
rules.why: A short, vague request that appears to come from a senior person exploits hierarchy - staff act first and question later.
rules.advice: Verify identity by calling the person on a number you already know. Do not act on money or data requests from email alone.

values: can you help me with something
i need you to do something
i am in a meeting so
before i go into a meeting

examples: Hi, are you at your desk? I need you to handle a confidential payment, I'm in a meeting.
falsePositives: Genuine short notes from executives exist; the tell is a money/data request combined with secrecy and phone avoidance.
